statement: Five whole numbers have an even product and an odd sum. What is the largest possible number of odd numbers among the five?

choices.misconception: I thought an even product means every one of the numbers must be even.
I gave the smallest possible number of odd numbers instead of the largest.
I used only the even product, which allows four odd numbers, and forgot the sum must be odd.
I used only the odd sum, which allows five odd numbers, and forgot the product must be even.

hints: What does each condition say about how many numbers are odd?
Treat the two conditions separately. An even product needs at least one even number. An odd sum needs a certain parity for the count of odd numbers. Combine both.
So at most four numbers are odd, and the number of odd ones must itself be odd.

solutions.reliable: An even product needs at least one even number, so at most 4 of the five are odd. A sum is odd exactly when it contains an odd number of odd terms, so the count of odd numbers is 1, 3 or 5. The largest count meeting both conditions is 3, for example 1, 1, 1, 2, 2 with product 4 and sum 7. The transferable idea: turn each parity condition into a fact about how many odd numbers there are, then intersect.

whyOnTest: Parity questions test whether you combine every condition, and the wrong choices each come from using just one of them.
